lead: A flexible sensor is built on a plastic, rubber or paper backing, so the whole device bends and wraps around the surface it measures. That opens up skin patches, e-skin and smart packaging that rigid silicon cannot serve. But a bendable sensor drifts, and one reading is never the whole truth. Fusing several sensors — by weighted average, a complementary filter, a Kalman filter or voting — gives one estimate better than any single part.
prereq: You need: 5.7 for digital output and calibration, and Unit 1 for error analysis and the statistical treatment of measurement data.

blocks.text: A flexible sensor sits on a backing that bends: the sensing film, electrodes and wiring are all deposited on it, so the device wraps around a wrist, a pipe or a food packet. Rigid silicon cannot; it cracks at a fraction of a percent of strain.

Four substrates cover most work. Polyimide (PI) is an amber plastic usable to about 300 °C, so silver ink can be cured and parts soldered. PET is clear and cheap but softens near 80 °C, so keep processing below about 120 °C. PDMS is a silicone rubber that stretches past 100 % and follows skin. Paper is cheapest and suits single-use test strips.

Conductors are printed, not etched. Screen printing pushes paste through a mesh and lays tracks a few micrometres to about 25 µm thick; it is fast and runs roll-to-roll. Inkjet printing drops ink only where needed, with no mask, but tracks are thinner and less conductive. Silver ink gives the lowest resistance. Carbon ink is cheaper and inert, the usual choice for electrodes and printed resistors. PEDOT:PSS is a transparent, stretchable conducting polymer with much lower conductivity.

Encapsulation is not optional. Oxygen and water vapour oxidise the silver and swell the polymer, so resistance drifts and sensitivity falls. A parylene layer or laminated barrier a few micrometres thick holds the response steady for months. See 5.6 for the rigid-wafer version.

A printed strain gauge is a track of silver or carbon on the flexible film. Its gauge factor is GF = (ΔR/R)/ε, where R is the unstrained resistance in ohms, ΔR the change in ohms, and ε the strain in m/m. A printed silver track has GF of 2 to 5, close to metal foil (Unit 2).

A crack-based gauge is a thin metal or carbon film on PDMS, deliberately precracked. Stretching opens the cracks and lengthens the conducting path; releasing closes them. GF can exceed 1000, and some designs reach 10 000, but the response is nonlinear and hysteretic and works only to about 1 % strain.

A capacitive pressure pad is two printed electrodes on either side of a foam or PDMS dielectric. C = ε₀ε_r A/d, where ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m, ε_r is the relative permittivity, A the overlap area in m² and d the thickness in m. Pressing squeezes air out: d falls and ε_r rises, so C rises. Such pads map seat occupancy and bed pressure over a few kPa.

Printed silver or platinum tracks serve as RTDs; printed NTC paste with β of 3000 K to 4000 K serves as a thermistor. Dry ECG and EMG electrodes are printed Ag/AgCl on breathable film with no wet gel, so skin-electrode impedance is tens of kΩ at 10 Hz against a few kΩ for gel — the amplifier needs a high input impedance. Sweat patches read pH from a printed iridium oxide electrode and glucose from a printed enzyme electrode (5.10).

Ratings to quote: minimum bend radius and fatigue. A printed silver track on 25 µm polyimide survives a bend radius near 1 mm. After 1000 bend cycles to that radius, ΔR/R is usually a few percent, and crack-based gauges drift the most.
One sensor has blind spots, drifts, and a single failure ruins the reading. Fusion combines N readings into one estimate with lower uncertainty, wider coverage and redundancy against failure.

items: Data-level fusion combines raw samples before any processing, for example averaging two thermocouple outputs before linearising them.
Feature-level fusion extracts a feature from each sensor, then combines, for example heart rate from ECG and from a pulse oximeter.
Decision-level fusion lets each sensor decide first, then combines the decisions by voting.

blocks.text: The inverse-variance weighted average is the workhorse. Give each reading weight w = 1/σ², where σ is that sensor's standard deviation in its own units. Then
x̂ = Σ wᵢ xᵢ / Σ wᵢ     σ_fused = 1 / √(Σ wᵢ)
blocks.where: x̂ is the fused estimate; xᵢ is reading i; wᵢ = 1/σᵢ² in (units of x)⁻²; σ_fused is the standard deviation of the fused estimate, in the same units as x.

blocks.text: A complementary filter splits the job by frequency: x̂ₖ = α(x̂ₖ₋₁ + ω Δt) + (1 − α)aₖ, where ω is a rate in rad/s, aₖ an angle from the second sensor, Δt the sample interval in s, and α ≈ 0.98. It is standard for tilt from an accelerometer plus a gyroscope.

The scalar Kalman filter adds a changing state. Predict: x̂⁻ = x̂ₖ₋₁ and P⁻ = Pₖ₋₁ + Q. Update: K = P⁻/(P⁻ + R), x̂ₖ = x̂⁻ + K(zₖ − x̂⁻), Pₖ = (1 − K)P⁻. Here zₖ is the new measurement, Q the process-noise variance, R the measurement-noise variance, P the estimate variance and K the gain, between 0 and 1. A large R makes K small, so the filter trusts the model over the sensor.
Majority voting needs an odd count: with three sensors, take the value two agree on. Dempster–Shafer theory combines belief masses when full probabilities cannot be assigned.

figure.caption: Sensor 2 has the smaller standard deviation, so its weight is 25 against 4 and the fused value lands close to 30.8 °C, not halfway between the two readings.

spec.title: Weighted fusion of two readings
spec.aria: Two temperature sensors with different uncertainties entering a weighting block that produces the fused value of 30.7 degrees Celsius.

examples.question: Two temperature sensors measure the same point. Sensor 1 reads 30.0 °C with σ₁ = 0.5 °C; sensor 2 reads 30.8 °C with σ₂ = 0.2 °C. The errors are independent and unbiased. (a) Find the inverse-variance weighted fused estimate. (b) Find the standard deviation of the fused estimate and compare it with the better sensor alone.
steps: Weight of a sensor is the inverse of its variance: w = 1/σ².
Fused estimate: T = 890/29 = 30.69 °C. The noisier sensor barely moves the result.
Compare: the better sensor alone gave 0.20 °C, so the gain is small because σ₂ already dominates. With two sensors at σ = 0.5 °C, fusion would give 0.5/√2 = 0.35 °C, a clear gain.
examples.answer: The fused estimate is 30.69 °C with σ_fused ≈ 0.19 °C; the weights are 4 °C⁻² and 25 °C⁻².
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction
T1, T2 = Fraction(300, 10), Fraction(308, 10)
s1, s2 = Fraction(5, 10), Fraction(2, 10)
w1 = 1 / s1**2
w2 = 1 / s2**2
ws = w1 + w2
Tf = (w1 * T1 + w2 * T2) / ws
sigma = (1 / float(ws)) ** 0.5
print(float(w1))
print(float(w2))
print(round(float(Tf), 2))
print(round(sigma, 2))

traps: Averaging two readings 50/50 when their uncertainties differ. The weight is 1/σ², not 1/σ.
Forgetting that correlated errors survive averaging. Two sensors on the same board share self-heating and the same reference voltage, so their common offset is not reduced at all.
Mixing up standard deviation and variance in the weight formula, or dropping the unit of weight, which is the inverse square of the measured quantity.
Confusing bend radius with bend angle. A smaller radius is the harsher test; a device rated at 5 mm may fail at 1 mm after the same number of cycles.
Assuming a crack-based gauge is linear over its whole range. Its gauge factor is huge but the response saturates beyond about 1 % strain.

quiz.q: Name two flexible substrates and give the approximate upper temperature each tolerates.
quiz.a: Polyimide, usable to about 300 °C. PET, usable below about 120 °C because it softens near 80 °C.

quiz.q: Why is encapsulation needed on a printed flexible sensor?
quiz.a: Oxygen and water vapour oxidise the silver tracks and swell the polymer film, changing resistance and sensitivity, so the reading drifts. A parylene or laminated barrier keeps the response stable for months.

quiz.q: A capacitive pressure pad uses a foam dielectric. Explain why its capacitance rises when you press it.
quiz.a: Pressing reduces the thickness d and squeezes air out, so the effective ε_r rises because air (ε_r ≈ 1) is replaced by foam material. Both changes increase C = ε₀ε_r A/d.

quiz.q: Sensor A reads 25.0 °C with σ_A = 1.0 °C; sensor B reads 26.0 °C with σ_B = 0.5 °C. Errors are independent. Find the weights, the fused estimate and its standard deviation.
Three sensors read 30.1 °C, 30.2 °C and 45.0 °C. Apply majority voting and state the result and its weakness.
quiz.a: Two readings agree near 30 °C, so the voted result is about 30.1–30.2 °C and 45.0 °C is rejected. Weakness: if two sensors share the same fault, the vote confirms the wrong value.

quiz.q: Two identical temperature sensors sit on the same board next to the same regulator. Their readings are averaged. Explain why the fused uncertainty is not 1/√2 times the single-sensor uncertainty.
quiz.a: The 1/√2 gain needs independent errors. Here both sensors share self-heating and the same supply reference, so errors are correlated. Averaging cancels only the independent random part and leaves the common offset untouched.

quiz.q: In a scalar Kalman filter, R is made very large while Q stays small. Describe what K does and what the output follows.
quiz.a: K = P⁻/(P⁻ + R) becomes close to zero. The update barely moves from the prediction, so the filter ignores the noisy measurements and follows its internal model.

quiz.q: State the difference between feature-level and decision-level fusion, with one example of each.
quiz.a: Feature-level fusion extracts a feature from each sensor and combines them, for example heart rate from ECG and from a pulse oximeter. Decision-level fusion lets each sensor decide, then combines decisions, for example three gas sensors voting 'leak' or 'no leak'.

beyond: Not for the exam. Flexible hybrid electronics print the wiring on plastic and solder only the bare ICs, which makes single-use medical patches and smart labels cheap. Research on e-skin stacks pressure, temperature and humidity sensors in elastomer layers and fuses them at feature level. Robotics, drones and battery management systems fuse inertial or cell data the same way. Search next for stretchable conductors, crack-based strain sensors, and the extended Kalman filter.
